wecert · architecture + lifecycle

From “somebody added a line to a DNS zone” to “deleted from the cloud”

The one rule everything else follows: wecert never infers. Something else works out what should exist and writes it down; wecert only reads that document and converges. The seven diagrams below go from the problem it solves down to the state machine of a single order.

ⓐ Deployment ① System map ② Intent → contract ③ Reconcile decisions ④ Order state machine ⑤ DNS-01 sequence ⑥ Life of a certificate Data ownership Failure semantics Rate-limit arithmetic Pitfalls

diagram ⓐDeployment shape: a free certificate rotating itself on the CLB

The band on top is the scenario this system exists for: a free certificate is valid for 90 days, so it has to rotate automatically — and why the choice falls on Let’s Encrypt rather than Tencent Cloud’s own free DV: those are single-domain certificates, supporting neither SAN nor wildcard, so every extra domain means another rotation to maintain. One Let’s Encrypt certificate holds up to 100 names and does support wildcards, so several domains combine into one certificate and rotate as one. The two bands below are what that scenario looks like on Tencent Cloud — the request path on top, and where the certificate comes from underneath. The relationship in the middle is the one that matters: SNI decides which certificate the CLB uses, and that certificate’s SAN decides which domains it can complete a handshake for — so domains sharing one certificate share its fate.

One easily missed consequence of this shape: the backend RSs take no part in TLS at all — decryption happens at the CLB, so the certificate is a cloud resource, not a few files. Putting certbot on every RS buys nothing, and tools that assume “the certificate ends up in a Secret” have nowhere to land here.

The other is that domains sharing one certificate share its fate. SNI only decides which certificate is used; what decides whether a domain can actually be served is that certificate’s SAN. So once a and b are in the same certificate, a DNS problem on a drags b down with it. That is the constraint the grouping policy, wildcard-first and the failure fallback are all built around (see diagram ② and table B).

diagram ①System map — who owns what, who only reads

Left to right is the transfer of authority: intent (written by a human) → inference (disposable) → contract (machine-written) → execution (must be stable) → external. Each layer has a different failure mode, and that is exactly why they are separated.

Human / upstream / declarations wecert-owned components the contract (the only interface between them) external services persistent state synchronous asynchronous optional critical path

Why put a file in the middle

If wecert enumerated DNS and CLB itself, it would be passively watching two side effects to infer intent. The problem is not accuracy, it is the failure mode: one DNS API hiccup returning empty gets read as “these names are gone”, and it reissues a certificate without them — the site stops handshaking.

With a document in between, a source failure becomes the desired state stops updating — and staying put is safe. Inference logic (new sources, new thresholds, new edge cases) will keep changing; the certificate lifecycle must not. Fusing the two would mean every change to inference is a change to issuance.

diagram ②Intent → contract: the inference pipeline

The six stages wecert-onboard runs in one pass. Note that red is only attached where a freeze actually happens — a failure in stage 2 or 3 is local and does not freeze the run.

Wildcard-first: this is where the quota is saved

The marginal cost of declaring *.example.com
ActionWithout a wildcardWith *.example.com
Add foo.example.com1 re-issuance0 the SAN set does not change
Import 50 subdomains50 → the weekly allowance is gone0
Add a.b.example.com1 re-issuance1 — needs *.b.example.com
Add example.net1 re-issuance1 — a different registered domain is a different certificate

A wildcard is never invented. Declaring *.example.com means the certificate can complete a handshake for any subdomain — that is a privilege expansion, and it has to be an explicit declaration rather than something the grouping logic decides on your behalf. For the same reason *.example.com does not cover example.com; both need declaring.

diagram ③Reconcile decisions — what each pass asks about a certificate

The checks are ordered. The first branch that matches decides what this pass does, and if none match the answer is “do nothing” — which is what happens on the overwhelming majority of passes.

Three invariants decide that order. (1) At most one in-flight order per certificate, and the order URL is on disk before anything else happens. (2) Renewals are ARI-first and carry replaces. (3) A wildcard and its apex share one _acme-challenge name, so the TXT records are written together, verified together and cleaned up together. Breaking any of them runs straight into 5 certificates per exact set of identifiers / 7 days — and that limit has no override.

diagram ④Order state machine — where a restart picks up

The entire point of this state machine is that the process can be killed at any moment. Every state has a column in state.db, and those columns decide, after a restart, whether to carry on or to place a new order.

The order URL must be on disk immediately after newOrder returns, before anything else. That is the whole of the crash-safety story: without it, a process killed during the few minutes of DNS propagation would place a second order whose identifier set is identical to the first — straight into the exact-set limit, with no override available.

The same reasoning explains why an order’s identifier set is stored separately: it is fixed when the order is created. If the configuration changes in the meantime, the correct action is to discard and rebuild the order, not to honour “never create a new order” and keep advancing one whose CSR can no longer finalize.

diagram ⑤DNS-01 — a wildcard and its apex share one TXT name

This is the easiest part to get wrong and the hardest to notice. example.com and *.example.com both put their challenge at _acme-challenge.example.com — one name, two values.

Why it has to be “write all → verify all → clean up together”

Handling identifiers one at a time — write, verify, clean, next — means the value written for *.example.com gets removed or overwritten before example.com is reached. DNSPod allows several TXT records under one name, but the cleanup has to happen together, or a challenge that already verified becomes invalid again.

Propagation checking uses a quorum rather than “every authoritative nameserver reachable”: in practice one of nine is routinely unreachable (measured: 8 confirm, 0 deny, 1 unreachable). Demanding all of them would never pass. The criterion is no reachable nameserver denies it, and at least one confirms — with multiple authorities at least 2 must confirm independently, and a zone with a single authority passes on one.

diagram ⑥The life of one certificate (classic, 90 days)

The axis is drawn for a classic 90-day certificate. What actually decides when renewal happens is ARI’s suggestedWindow; renewBefore below it is only the fallback for when ARI is unavailable.

What changing the profile changes

The three ACME profiles
ProfileValidityMax NamesDefault renewBefore
classic (default)90 days10030 days
tlsserver45 days2515 days
shortlived160 hours2548 hours

The CA/Browser Forum has scheduled ≤100 days from 2027-03-15 and ≤47 days from 2029-03-15, so “90 days plus a manual fallback” stops being an option within two years. The desired-state generator caps a certificate at 25 names by default (aligned with tlsserver) so that switching profiles later needs no redesign.

table BFailure semantics — every kind of “cannot read it” has a defined reaction

This table is the heart of the design. None of these treats “unreadable” as “gone”.

Situation → reaction → why
SituationReactionWhy
Declaration source unreadable (DNS API hiccup, permissions changed) freeze the whole run the document is untouched Empty is not the same as gone; acting on it would reissue a certificate with no names
CLB guard unreadable no deletions at all and the guard counts as satisfied Degrading makes safety disappear along with the dependency, exactly when you need it most
Document unreadable (runtime) freeze on the last revision and keep renewing from it Renewals continue; only new names stop arriving
Document unreadable (startup · enforce) hard failure, does not start Failing to start is loud; “starts but renews nothing” is silent
Document unreadable (startup · observe) falls back to static with a clear warning While observing, the document not existing yet is normal and must not stop the process
The desired state computes to empty refuse to write -force does not override A legitimate empty state and a failed generation look identical in the file
Declared set drops by more than 30% freeze + alert A normal decommission does not lose a third; losing a third means the upstream collapsed
More than 25 name-set changes in 7 days freeze + alert Let’s Encrypt allows 50 per registered domain per 7 days, shared across accounts
Removing a name only when all three hold Confirmed absent + past 24h + unreferenced by any CLB rule
A group exceeds 25 SANs keep that group’s previous revision Dropping the group would show wecert a certificate that vanished
One declaration is malformed (unknown key) exclude just that one with a reason in the report A single typo must not stop every certificate from updating
One certificate fails to issue does not affect the others One misconfigured certificate holding up every renewal is the most dangerous coupling in automation
Near expiry and issuance keeps failing (failureFallback on) drop the names that keep failing and sign the rest Partial availability beats total failure. Only names with evidence of individual failure are dropped; once that record ages out the name is no longer dropped, but the full set is only retried at the next renewal window

table CThe rate-limit arithmetic — why wildcard-first is not an optimisation

Let's Encrypt rate limits (the ones this system runs into)
LimitAllowanceWhen you hit itHow to avoid it
New Orders / account300 / 3 hoursRe-placing ordersPersist the order URL and reuse it after a crash
New Certs / registered domain50 / 7 days · shared across accountsFrequent changes to the name setWildcard-first plus a 25-changes-per-week budget
New Certs / exact identifier set5 / 7 days · no overrideReissuing the same name set repeatedlyAt most one in-flight order per certificate
Authorization Failures / identifier5 / hourRetrying a name whose DNS is not configuredBackoff, then hand over to a human
ARI-coordinated renewals: exempt from all of the above. The order must carry replaces and share at least one identifier with the certificate it replaces — an unchanged set trivially qualifies; only a wholly disjoint set loses the exemption.

That last row is what makes wildcard-first more than an optimisation: a domain set wholly disjoint from the old certificate is a brand-new certificate, which forfeits the ARI exemption and spends “Certificates per Registered Domain (50 / 7 days)” instead (adding or removing a domain keeps the exemption as long as at least one identifier is shared). The cost of “add one domain” therefore has to be driven to nearly zero, and a wildcard is the only way to do that. It is also why the desired-state generator prefers to report “covered by the declared wildcard, 0 issuances” over touching the SAN set.

table DField notes and pitfalls

All found by actually running this, ordered by how much time they would waste you.

Enabling SNI on a CLB silently ignores the primary certificate field

You must write multi_cert_info. And only the CertificateDeployInstanceEmpty error code exposes it — otherwise everything looks fine.

DescribeListeners does not read certificate bindings back

The reliable independent signals are UpdateSyncProgress.TotalCount in the UpdateCertificateInstance response and CreateCertificateBindResourceSyncTask — the latter is also what wecert uses on every pass to confirm a hand-bound certificate. A TotalCount of 0 means the certificate was never actually bound.

Uploading is not binding

The rebind is asynchronous — measured at about 15 seconds — and not atomic. deploy_confirmed is only set once the switch is confirmed; otherwise the first upload would turn the deployed gauge green and the expiry alarm would think everything is fine.

In the binding status, 1 is “done”

The Status semantics of CreateCertificateBindResourceSyncTask are easy to guess backwards (0 = done is wrong). Guessing backwards looks like “the task never completes”.

The CSR must be DER, and posted to the finalize URL

Sending PEM gets you asn1 tags don’t match; posting to the order URL gets you POST-as-GET requests must have an empty payload. lego’s parameter happens to be called orderURL, which makes it easy to hit.

Terraform will revert the certificate wecert bound

Both IaC and the runtime write the same field. The fix is a lifecycle { ignore_changes = [multi_cert_info, certificate_id] } on the CLB resource — at the cost of TF state staying stale.

DNSPod’s free tier has a TTL floor of 600

Writing 60 is rejected with LimitExceeded.RecordTtlLimit, so 600 is the default.

Propagation checking cannot require “every authoritative NS reachable”

In practice one of nine nameservers is always unreachable. The criterion is a quorum: no reachable nameserver denies it, and at least one confirms; with multiple authorities at least 2 must confirm independently, and a zone with a single authority passes on one.

CLB health-check source addresses are not in the VPC CIDR

It shows up as a 504 while the TLS handshake is actually fine — very easy to misdiagnose as a certificate problem. Widening the security group fixes it.
